title: Swap success and depth control
takeaway: Exchanging an unspoken intermediate concept for an alternative in J-lens coordinates moves the alternative's implied answer to the model's top-1 output on 54% of two-hop prompts for Haiku 4.5 and 70% for both Sonnet 4.5 and Opus 4.5. A depth comparison shows the intermediate swap takes effect a median of about 17% of depth earlier than a swap of the answer itself, which the paper takes as evidence that the intermediate is used before the answer is computed, not that its lens vector smuggles the answer in.
walkthrough:
This is a two-panel figure, rendered in the article as a live widget rather than a static image. Both panels score the same intervention: a [[lens-coordinate-swap]]. The swap reads an activation's coordinates along two [[j-lens-vector]] directions — the unspoken intermediate of a two-hop question, and a chosen alternative from the same category — exchanges the two coordinates at every token position, and leaves the rest of the activation untouched. If the intermediate is causally load-bearing, the model's final answer should follow the swapped-in concept.

The left panel gives the headline rates. Each bar is one model from the [[claude-model-family]], and its height is the [[swap-success-rate]]: the fraction of 50 two-hop factual prompts, drawn like the [[multihop-benchmark]], on which the swap moved the swap-appropriate answer to the top of the output distribution. The criterion is strict. Success means the implied answer becomes the single most likely next token out of the whole vocabulary. The rates are 54% on Haiku 4.5, 70% on Sonnet 4.5, and 70% on Opus 4.5.

The right panel is a control, the paper's [[swap-depth-control]]. The worry is a confound: the intermediate's lens vector might already correlate with the answer's vector — spider might carry some 8 — so that swapping spider for ant works only because it incidentally swaps in some 6. The test compares two interventions applied over different layer ranges: swapping the intermediate versus swapping the answer directly. The y-axis is the log-probability difference in the expected output; the x-axis is depth, with layers reindexed 0–100 under the paper's [[layer-percentage-indexing]] convention. Curves are computed over successful Sonnet 4.5 trials, with a shaded standard-error band.

The logic: if the intermediate swap worked through a smuggled-in answer component, both curves would rise at the same depth. They do not. The intermediate swap takes effect a median of approximately 17% of depth earlier than the answer swap. From this separation, the paper concludes that the model represents and makes use of the intermediate concept before the answer has been computed — the causal chain runs through the intermediate, supporting the [[internal-reasoning]] property of the workspace.

terms.definition: The left panel's y-axis: the share of two-hop prompts on which a lens-coordinate swap of the unspoken intermediate moved the swap-implied answer to the very top of the model's next-token distribution.
The success criterion: the swap-appropriate answer must become the single most likely next token out of the entire vocabulary, not merely rise in probability.
The smallest of the three production Claude models evaluated; the left panel shows it with the lowest swap success rate, 54%.
The mid-size Claude model and the paper's default subject; it reaches 70% swap success, and the right panel's depth comparison is computed on its successful trials.
The largest of the three Claude models evaluated; it matches Sonnet 4.5 at 70% swap success.

Exchanging the J-lens coordinates of the unspoken intermediate concept (for example spider) for an alternative from the same category, at all token positions, leaving the rest of the activation fixed.

The right panel's comparison intervention: the same coordinate exchange applied to the answer tokens themselves (for example 8 and 6) rather than to the intermediate. It serves as the reference for where in depth a direct answer manipulation acts.
The right panel's y-axis: how much a swap applied at a given layer range shifts the log-probability of the swap-implied answer. A large value means the swap is doing causal work at those layers.

The right panel's x-axis: which layers the swap is applied at. The paper samples 25 evenly spaced layers of the residual stream and reindexes them to 0–100, so layer numbers read as percentages of model depth.
The shaded band around each curve in the right panel: the standard error of the mean log-prob difference across the successful trials.
The subset of prompts on which the swap succeeded by the top-1 criterion; the right panel's curves are averaged over these Sonnet 4.5 trials only.
The evaluation set: 50 factual questions whose correct answer requires first inferring an unspoken bridging concept, such as inferring spider before reporting its number of legs.

numbers.meaning: Swap success rate on Haiku 4.5: the fraction of the 50 two-hop prompts on which swapping the intermediate's lens coordinates moved the swap-implied answer to top-1. The smallest model shows the weakest effect.

Swap success rate on Sonnet 4.5, and identically on Opus 4.5: on seven in ten two-hop prompts the coordinate swap redirects the model's top output to the answer implied by the swapped-in intermediate.
The number of two-hop factual prompts with known intermediates in the evaluation set behind the left panel; the swap target is chosen at random from the same category as the true intermediate.

The median amount of depth (in the paper's 0–100 layer indexing) by which the intermediate swap takes effect earlier than the answer swap in the right panel. If the intermediate's lens vector merely contained a copy of the answer, both swaps would act at the same depth; the separation is the paper's evidence that the intermediate is used before the answer exists.
The layer index range on the right panel's depth axis: 25 evenly spaced residual-stream layers reindexed so that layer numbers read as percentages of the model's depth.
The rank the swap-implied answer must reach for a trial to count as a success: it must become the model's single most likely next token.
